name: Expensify
tagline: Expense management platform with receipt scanning and reporting.
description: Expensify reads receipts with SmartScan, runs them through multi-level approval chains, and posts finished expense data to your accounting system.
pros: SmartScan reads merchant name, date, amount, and category off a receipt photo, so submission does not start with typing
Approval chains, policy enforcement rules, and automatic categorization are recorded as one workflow engine rather than three separate settings
Expense data transfers to QuickBooks, Xero, and Sage Intacct, leaving the general ledger in the accounting system the company already runs
Corporate card reconciliation, mileage tracking, and per-diem management sit alongside receipt capture instead of in a second tool
The finance buyers' guide in this repository models Expensify at $9 per user per month inside a 20-person stack, which stays inside the recorded band
cons: Expensify carries expenses, not the books: invoicing, bank reconciliation, and financial statements stay in whatever ledger receives its transfers
Price records disagree — this page holds a $5-9/mo band while the repository's expense comparison states that none of the platforms it covers had verified pricing

content.title: Where Expensify sits in a finance stack
content.body: This repository's finance buyers' guide describes a small-business stack as four layers — accounting, invoicing, expense, and payroll — and keeps dedicated expense tools on their own layer rather than inside the ledger. The same guide argues that receipt capture built into an accounting product is sufficient while a team stays under roughly 25 employees, and that larger teams move to a dedicated expense tool such as Expensify. Our finance category page draws the line from the other direction, recording spend management as a category that combines corporate cards, expense management, and accounts payable automation, with Expensify named beside Brex and Ramp as one of the platforms that created it. Read from that position, Expensify is the part of the stack that collects and polices spending before it reaches the books.

content.title: SmartScan and what comes off a receipt
content.body: The expense-management comparison stored in this repository makes SmartScan the defining capability: a receipt photo is read, and the merchant name, date, amount, and category are pulled off it, which removes typed entry from the submission path. The same entry records the capture options wrapped around it — corporate card reconciliation, mileage tracking, and per-diem expense management — so a claim travels with whatever evidence documents it. Our accounting-selection guide describes the buyer-side version of the problem: a business where many employees submit expenses needs expense handling of its own, or an integration with a dedicated expense tool. What no record here shows is the product exercising judgment on an employee's behalf; scanning produces fields, and approval is still the step that decides.

content.title: Approval chains and policy rules
content.body: Submission is only the half of the expense flow that the comparison in this repository describes; the other half is what happens afterward. Its approval workflow engine is recorded as supporting multi-level chains, enforcing policy rules, and filling in expense categories automatically — the portion a finance lead audits before money leaves the account. The workflow pieces on file are:
items: Multi-level approval chains routing an expense past more than one reviewer
Policy enforcement rules checked while expenses are submitted
Automatic categorization applied once a receipt has been scanned
Corporate card transactions reconciled against the receipts behind them
Mileage and per-diem claims carried through the same approval path

content.title: Sending finished expenses to the ledger
content.body: An expense tool that cannot reach the accounting system leaves someone retyping totals, which is why the recorded integration path carries weight. The expense comparison in this repository names three destinations for Expensify data — QuickBooks, Xero, and Sage Intacct — and describes the transfer as moving expense data into those accounting systems. That list matches how the rest of this repository treats them: QuickBooks and Xero as small-business ledgers, Sage Intacct as the multi-entity option for larger operations. The accounting-selection guide makes the same dependency explicit, framing expense capture as either native to the accounting product or connected through a dedicated tool, and it is in the second route that Expensify is filed.

content.title: What the price record says about Expensify
content.body: This review's own fields record Expensify as freemium with a list band of $5-9/mo. Two other records in the repository qualify that figure instead of confirming it: the expense-management comparison states that none of the platforms it covers carried published pricing verification at the time of writing and directs readers to each vendor's current pricing page, while the finance buyers' guide models Expensify at $9 per user per month inside an example stack for a 20-person company, which sits at the top of the recorded band. Several of Expensify's own comparison records in this dataset store no starting price at all. The result is a band held by this page and a warning attached to it, so treat the range as recorded rather than quoted.

content.title: What expense capture does not do
content.body: Three limits follow from what Expensify is. It does not hold the general ledger: invoicing, bank reconciliation, and financial statements belong to whichever accounting system receives its transfers, which is why this repository's guides discuss Expensify as an addition to a ledger rather than a replacement for one. The boundaries of the free tier are not established anywhere in these records, so a buyer evaluating cost has a band and no documented plan structure behind it. Nothing on file answers what happens to a receipt image after its fields are extracted — retention, storage location, and deletion are unrecorded here — so that question belongs in the vendor conversation rather than on this page.

content.title: Cloud delivery, API, and the certification record
content.body: The data assembled for this page records Expensify as delivered from the cloud with an API field that is marked available, which fits an expense flow that begins on a phone and ends in someone else's accounting system: receipt images leave the submitting device, and the approval record is held by the vendor rather than on a local install. What this repository does not carry is a compliance certification of any kind for Expensify, and no security or privacy attestation appears in the records behind this page either. Absence here means the dataset holds nothing, not that the product fails any standard. A buyer whose sign-off depends on certification evidence should request current documentation directly from the vendor.

content.title: How the comparison records read Expensify
content.body: Sixteen comparison records in this repository pair Expensify with another product. The rows place it ahead of BigCommerce, FullStory, Paddle, PayPal, QuickBooks, Sage Intacct, Sage, Wave, and WooCommerce, and behind BambooHR, FreshBooks, Shopify, Square, Stripe, Xero, and Zoho Books — a mixed field where several of the losses are category mismatches, since Stripe, Shopify, and Square are payments or commerce products rather than expense tools.

content.title: Who should put expenses on Expensify
content.body: The recorded buyer is an organization where expense submission is a recurring problem rather than an occasional one: this repository's finance guide raises Expensify only after a team passes roughly 25 employees, and the accounting-selection guide raises it when many employees are submitting expenses. Inside a company that points at three roles — staff who travel or buy on a company card, a manager who signs off on those claims, and a finance function that wants categorized entries arriving in the ledger instead of a shoebox of photos. The recorded integration list narrows the fit again: a company already running QuickBooks, Xero, or Sage Intacct follows the documented path, while one on an unlisted accounting product would be depending on an integration these records do not describe.

content.title: Fit, and where these statements come from
content.body: Expensify's fit is narrow and consistent across the records: a receipt-and-approval layer feeding an existing ledger, filed here as freemium at $5-9/mo, carrying a rating of 4.2 out of 5 from 1,360 reviews on this page. It is the wrong instrument for a company that needs the books themselves, and an unnecessary one for a very small team whose accounting product already photographs receipts. The statements above were assembled from stored material rather than from use — the expense-management comparison, the finance and accounting guides, and the fields attached to this review. Where two of those records disagree, the disagreement is stated rather than resolved.

faqs.question: Does Expensify replace accounting software?
faqs.answer: No. The finance guide in this repository treats it as a dedicated expense layer, and the expense comparison records transfers into QuickBooks, Xero, and Sage Intacct rather than a general ledger of its own.

faqs.question: What does SmartScan read from a receipt?
faqs.answer: Four fields are recorded: merchant name, date, amount, and category, extracted from a receipt photo so the employee does not retype them before approval.

faqs.question: Who approves an expense in Expensify before it posts?
faqs.answer: Approval chains are recorded as multi-level, with policy enforcement rules running alongside them and categorization filled in automatically once a receipt has been scanned.

faqs.question: What price does this page record for Expensify?
faqs.answer: A freemium model with a band of $5-9/mo, alongside a warning from the repository's expense comparison that none of the platforms it covers had verified pricing and that the vendor's current page should be checked.

faqs.question: Which alternatives does this repository suggest for Expensify?
faqs.answer: Wave, Zoho Books, and Sage Intacct appear in its comparison records alongside QuickBooks, Xero, FreshBooks, and Stripe, though several of those pairings are category mismatches rather than like-for-like swaps.

author: Emily Nakamura
learningCurve: Moderate — expect 1-3 days to become productive
whoShouldUse: Organizations where many employees submit expenses and a ledger already exists elsewhere: the recorded path runs receipt capture, approval under policy rules, and transfer into QuickBooks, Xero, or Sage Intacct.
whoShouldNotUse: Teams under roughly 25 people whose accounting product already photographs receipts, and buyers who need a general ledger, invoicing, or financial statements rather than an expense layer feeding one.
